sections.title: The Challenge
points: Each write can update durable data, indexes, and replicas. Shared invariants can also force writes to run in sequence.
Find the busiest constrained component. Adding application servers does not remove a single hot row or storage bottleneck.

sections.title: 1) Vertical scaling and write optimization
points: Measure CPU, memory, disk, and network limits before adding distribution. Better hardware can provide useful capacity with less architectural complexity.
Shorten transactions, reuse connections, and remove unnecessary write work. Batch operations when their ordering and durability rules permit it.
B-tree and log-structured engines make different tradeoffs. Sequential writes can improve throughput but leave more read or compaction work.
Cassandra, time-series stores, and column stores fit different workloads. Choose from required operations and durability, not a generic SQL-versus-NoSQL label.

sections.title: 2) Sharding and partitioning
points: Horizontal sharding spreads records across write owners. Redis Cluster, for example, maps hashed key slots to server nodes.
Choose a key that spreads write traffic while keeping related reads local. A high number of possible keys alone does not ensure balance.
A country key can overload populous regions. Hashing user IDs often distributes work better, but unusually active users still need attention.
Vertical partitioning separates fields with different workloads. Post content, engagement counters, and analytics can use different stores or tables.
Check how many shards each common read and write touches. Cross-shard operations add coordination, network calls, and failure cases.

flows.title: Route a Redis Cluster write to its slot owner
steps: The Redis Client obtains the cluster's key-slot ownership map.
It hashes the requested key to determine the slot.
It sends the write to the server that owns that slot.
It refreshes routing information when ownership changes or the cluster redirects the request.

sections.title: 3) Queues and load shedding
points: Kafka or SQS can buffer a short write burst. Workers drain accepted requests at a rate the database can sustain.
A queue cannot fix permanent undercapacity. If arrivals remain faster than processing, both backlog size and completion delay keep growing.
Queue acknowledgement means acceptance, not database completion. Provide a status path when callers need to know that the write finished.
Shed or defer lower-priority writes before overload causes broader failure. For repeated location updates, a later update may replace an older one.

flows.title: Accept a burst and drain the write queue
steps: The App Server validates the request and submits accepted work to the Write Queue.
It waits for the required queue acknowledgement before confirming acceptance to the caller.
A Worker reads the queued request and writes the result to the database.
It acknowledges progress only after the required output is safe.
The caller checks completion separately when needed. Queue age must remain bounded by capacity and admission policy.

sections.title: 4) Batching and aggregation
points: Batching combines small writes to reduce network, transaction, and storage overhead. It adds a delay before the combined operation runs.
Batch in an application or intermediate processor. Do not acknowledge volatile buffered data as durable unless a replayable source retains it.
A Like Batcher combines increments per post. Hierarchical Write Processors can aggregate local changes before a Root Processor merges them.
Broadcast Nodes then distribute the shared result to their clients. Retry and ordering rules must prevent repeated batches from duplicating effects.
Larger batches improve efficiency only when work combines usefully. One like per post per window provides little aggregation benefit.

diagrams.caption: Fan-In, Fan-Out Problem of Live Comments

flows.title: Combine like events before database writes
steps: Kafka receives individual like events.
The Like Batcher groups events by post during a chosen window.
It emits combined like-count changes into the downstream Kafka topic.
A consumer applies those changes to the Likes DB with the required retry protection.
The window trades fewer writes for delayed visibility. Sparse posts may gain little from this batch.

flows.title: Aggregate updates through a processing hierarchy
steps: Clients send comments and likes to Write Processors selected by the relevant comment ID.
Each Write Processor combines local changes over a short window.
The Root Processor merges the batches into a shared update.
Broadcast Nodes receive that update and forward it to their assigned clients.
Each layer handles less traffic than a single all-to-all processor, at the cost of additional delay.

sections.title: When to Use
points: This pattern fits telemetry, click processing, search ingestion, feed updates, and live comments. Each can produce more writes than one component handles.
Estimate normal and peak traffic. Identify whether storage I/O, CPU, network, lock contention, or one key causes the limit.
Start with a simpler fix when it meets the requirement. Sharding and queues add failure modes and operational work.

sections.title: 1) Resharding
points: Reshard gradually while the system remains available. The source proposes copying records while writes reach both old and new locations.
Dual writes can partially fail. Track and reconcile migration progress before moving read preference or write ownership permanently.
Consistent hashing reduces how many keys move. It does not itself copy data or protect concurrent updates during migration.

flows.title: Migrate records while writes continue
steps: The system selects the destination shards and records the migration boundaries.
It copies existing records while routing new changes to both old and new locations under the chosen migration protocol.
It tracks partial write failures and reconciles the destination until it reaches the required state.
Reads prefer the verified destination as ownership transitions. Stale routes need explicit forwarding or rejection behavior.
Retire the old copy only after validation and the rollback policy permit it. Dual writes alone do not guarantee a lossless migration.

sections.title: 2) Hot keys
points: More shards do not divide writes to one key. A viral post can overload even a shard dedicated to that post.
Split an additive counter into subkeys and combine their values during reads. This trades lower write contention for more read work.
Split only hot keys when useful. Readers and writers must agree on all active subkeys before the transition can preserve totals.
Some operations cannot be split independently, such as claiming one specific seat. Keep an authoritative owner and control incoming demand.

flows.title: Split an additive counter across subkeys
steps: Writers and readers agree on the subkeys used for the logical counter.
Each writer chooses one subkey and applies its increment there.
A reader fetches all active subkeys and combines their values.
A dynamic split updates routing before new subkeys receive writes. Retried increments still need protection against duplicate application.

sections.title: Conclusion
points: Reduce work per component through local optimization, partitioning, queues, or aggregation. Choose only strategies compatible with the required semantics.
Monitor queue age, partition load, retries, and storage or replication lag. Total throughput can hide one overloaded component.
Explain the delay, freshness, and correctness cost of each scaling choice. Higher throughput alone does not establish a successful design.
